title: Is Your Android Phone Hacked? How to Check and What to Do
html:
Strange behaviour on a phone has more than one possible cause: an unwanted app, spam notifications from a website, or someone using one of your accounts. Check them in this order. First scan with Play Protect and look at the apps on the phone. Then try Safe mode. Then secure your Google account. A factory reset comes last.

Last updated: 10 Oct 2026. Menu names vary by brand and Android version; use the Settings search box if you cannot find one.

I walked through these screens on a vivo V23 Pro running Android 14 (Funtouch OS 14, security update January 2025) on 11 Oct 2026. On my phone, Device admin apps is under Settings, then Apps, then Special app access, and also under Settings, then Security. Mine said "No active apps". Install unknown apps is on the same Special app access screen. My Google Account's Your devices page showed my phone and my Windows computer, with one older session signed out.

What odd behaviour can and cannot tell you

Pop-up ads outside any app, apps you do not remember installing, a battery that drains faster than before, or a security alert from Google are all reasons to check. None of them proves a hack on its own. A worn battery or a busy app can drain power too. Treat them as a prompt to look, not as a verdict.

1. Run Play Protect

Open the Play Store, tap your profile picture, then tap Play Protect. Google says Play Protect checks your apps and devices for harmful behaviour, warns you about potentially harmful apps, and may deactivate or remove them. It is on by default. Make sure "Scan apps with Play Protect" is switched on in its settings, and run a scan from that screen.

If it flags an app, uninstall it. For more on what the screen means, see our Play Protect guide.

2. Look at the apps on the phone

Go to Settings, then Apps, then See all apps. Look for anything you did not install or cannot explain. Then check two special settings.

  • Install unknown apps: Settings, then Apps, then Special app access, then Install unknown apps. This lists the apps that are allowed to install other apps from outside the Play Store. Most people should see none, apart from a browser or file manager they chose.
  • Accessibility: open Settings, then Accessibility, and look at the apps listed there. An accessibility service can read what is on your screen and act for you. Google explains that Android may block these settings for apps you installed from outside the Play Store, and that you can allow them with "Allow restricted settings" on an app's info page. Google's own warning is: "We don't recommend that you allow restricted settings unless you trust the app developer." If someone on a call or in a message told you to switch this on, do not.

3. Try Safe mode

Safe mode starts the phone with only its built-in apps. Google's steps for removing unwanted software: boot into Safe mode (usually by pressing and holding the power button, then touching and holding "Power off"; some phones differ), then remove recently downloaded apps one by one, restarting normally after each one, until the problem stops. If the problem goes away in Safe mode, an app you installed is the likely cause.

More detail is in our Safe mode guide.

On my vivo V23 Pro, pressing and holding Power off in the power menu opens a "Reboot to safe mode" box with Cancel and OK buttons. I tapped Cancel, so I have not tested how to leave Safe mode on this phone.

4. Pop-ups that come from a website

Some pop-ups are not an app at all but notifications from a website you allowed. In Chrome, open the site, tap Page info at the top left, tap Permissions, then Notifications, and turn "Show notifications" off.

5. Secure your Google account

A phone is often only the door to your accounts, so check the account too.

  1. Open your Google Account, go to Security, find the Your devices panel and choose Manage all devices. Tap any device or session you do not recognise and choose Sign out. Several sessions can share one device name, so you may need to sign out of more than one.
  2. Change your password, and change it anywhere else you used the same one.
  3. Turn on 2-Step Verification.
  4. In Gmail, check for forwarding rules and filters you did not create.

Our Google account security checklist walks through this in more detail.

If money or a one-time code is involved

Call your bank first, using the number on your card or in its official app, and freeze the card or UPI access if you can. Then report it. We keep the current reporting steps for India in one place, so they stay accurate. Do not install an app because a caller or message tells you to.

6. Last resort: factory reset

If the problem comes back after all of this, a factory reset erases everything on the phone and starts clean. Google says a factory reset erases all your data, that you need your Google Account details and screen lock to set the phone up again, and that you should back up first. After the reset, install your apps again from the Play Store instead of restoring apps you do not recognise.

What to do next

  1. Scan with Play Protect and uninstall what it flags.
  2. Check Install unknown apps and Accessibility for anything you did not set up.
  3. Use Safe mode to find a bad app, and turn off notifications from unknown websites.
  4. Sign out unknown devices from your Google account, change the password, and turn on 2-Step Verification.
  5. Reset only if the problem keeps coming back.
